title: Date and wartime context
short: Written in February 1915, before Thomas enlisted in July 1915; published in Poems (1917) under the pseudonym 'Edward Eastaway'.
body: Edward Thomas (1878-1917) began writing poetry only in late 1914, encouraged by Robert Frost. 'The Owl' dates from February 1915, months before he joined the Artists' Rifles in July 1915. Most of his poems were published after his death, in Poems (1917) under the pseudonym 'Edward Eastaway'. He was killed at Arras on 9 April 1917. The poem is not set at the front, but the war is present in its last line. It begins with a walker coming down a hill to an inn, a scene typical of Thomas's poetry of walking and rural England.

sources.cite: Edna Longley, ed., Edward Thomas: The Annotated Collected Poems (Tarset: Bloodaxe, 2008), notes to 'The Owl'

title: hungry ... Cold ... tired
short: Three conditions, each qualified by 'yet': hungry but not starved, cold but warm within, tired but not exhausted.
body: The first stanza lists three conditions, each qualified: 'hungry, and yet not starved; / Cold, yet had heat within me ...; tired, yet so that rest / Had seemed the sweetest thing'. The qualifications mark the walker's privileged state: his hardships are moderate and chosen. The triad returns in l. 6, 'how hungry, cold, and tired was I', and is implicitly contrasted with the unqualified hunger, cold and tiredness of those outside. The careful qualifying syntax is characteristic of Thomas.

title: proof / Against the North wind
short: 'Proof against' means impervious to, resistant to, as in 'armour proof against a sword'.
body: 'Proof' here is an adjective meaning able to withstand, impervious, as in 'proof against' attack, or the compound 'waterproof'. The OED records this sense from the sixteenth century, often of armour. The inner heat protects the walker from the north wind. The word has a slightly archaic, martial ring, faintly anticipating the soldiers of the last stanza. The sense is of a body that, for now, is well defended; by the end of the poem that self-sufficiency has been called into question.

title: food, fire, and rest
short: The inn supplies each need named in stanza 1: food for hunger, fire for cold, rest for tiredness.
body: The second stanza answers the first: 'food, fire, and rest' meets the hunger, cold and tiredness of the walk. The alliteration of 'food, fire' adds warmth. 'Knowing how hungry, cold, and tired was I' shows that the satisfaction makes him aware, for the first time, of the extent of his need. The shelter of the inn is set against the open night outside.

title: All of the night was quite barred out
short: The inn's shutters and doors bar out the night, except for one sound.
body: The night is 'quite barred out', excluded by the inn's walls and shutters. 'Quite' means completely. The one exception, the owl's cry, breaks the protective enclosure. The enjambment 'except / An owl's cry' runs across the stanza's line end, imitating the cry's intrusion. Thomas often sets an interior against the weather and the dark outside, and here the walls that should guarantee comfort prove unable to exclude what the owl brings in: knowledge of others' exposure. The phrase prepares the moral turn of the last two stanzas.

sources.cite: Neil Corcoran, ed., The Cambridge Companion to Twentieth-Century English Poetry (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2007), chapter on Owen, Sassoon and the poetry of war (reproduced at Literariness.org)

title: a most melancholy cry
short: The owl's cry is conventionally melancholy in English poetry, as in Gray's 'moping owl'.
body: The owl has long been the bird of night, death and melancholy in English poetry; Gray's 'Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard' has the 'moping owl' that 'does to the moon complain'. Thomas's phrase 'a most melancholy cry' is deliberately conventional and slightly archaic in its use of 'most'. The repetition 'An owl's cry, a most melancholy cry' extends the sound, as the next line's 'Shaken out long and clear' does. The Cambridge Companion chapter reads the cry as quietly undermining the poem's final rhyme.

title: No merry note
short: Answers Shakespeare's winter song, where the owl's cry is 'a merry note' (Love's Labour's Lost 5.2).
body: The winter song that ends Love's Labour's Lost has the lines 'Then nightly sings the staring owl, / Tu-whit, to-who, a merry note'. Thomas's owl gives 'No merry note, nor cause of merriment'. The Cambridge Companion chapter notes the contrast. Shakespeare's song depicts a rural winter of hardship ('When icicles hang by the wall') in a comic key; Thomas's owl brings the hardship of others into the warm inn without any merriment.

anchor: telling me plain what I escaped
title: telling me plain what I escaped
short: The owl's cry tells him plainly what he has escaped and others could not: shelter as luck, not merit.
body: The cry's message is 'plain', clear: it tells the speaker 'what I escaped / And others could not, that night'. The stress on escape and on others' inability shows the speaker's awareness of his privilege. 'That night, as in I went' places the moment exactly. The owl becomes a messenger of conscience. The plainness matters: the cry is not a supernatural omen or a Romantic symbol but a clear statement, and the speaker accepts its meaning without argument. The verb 'escaped' carries a faint sense of guilt, as if comfort were a kind of evasion.

title: salted
short: 'Salted' means seasoned, made sharp or poignant; also salt as tears; the owl's voice salts his comfort.
body: 'Salted' is the poem's key word, repeated: 'salted was my food, and my repose, / Salted and sobered'. Salt seasons food and gives it savour; the Cambridge Companion chapter glosses the sense as seasoned, but also made poignant or piquant. Salt also suggests tears and the sea. There may be a biblical undertone: in Mark 9:49, 'every one shall be salted with fire', and in Matthew 5:13 the faithful are 'the salt of the earth'. 'Sobered' adds seriousness: the comfort is not cancelled but chastened by awareness of others.

title: Speaking for all who lay under the stars
short: The owl speaks for those who sleep outside: it takes on the representative role the poet avoids claiming.
body: The owl's voice is 'Speaking for all who lay under the stars', those without shelter that night. The Cambridge Companion chapter observes that the owl speaks for others, sparing the poet the presumption of doing so directly: the owl is insistent, the poet is not. 'Under the stars' is gentle in phrasing but stark in implication: sleeping in the open, in winter.

title: Soldiers and poor
short: The lack of an article ('Soldiers and poor') may suggest that soldiers are themselves among the poor.
body: The last line names those for whom the owl speaks: 'Soldiers and poor, unable to rejoice'. The absence of 'the' before 'poor' makes the two groups run together, and the Cambridge Companion chapter suggests the phrasing may imply that soldiers are themselves poor, a politically pointed suggestion. In February 1915 soldiers were sleeping out in the trenches and in camps; Thomas would join them within months. The poem's voice contrasts with the patriotic note of Rupert Brooke's 'The Soldier' (1914).

title: Form: rhyme and ending
short: Four pentameter quatrains rhyming only on lines 2 and 4; the final rhyme 'voice' / 'rejoice' closes on inability.
body: The poem's four quatrains of loose iambic pentameter rhyme only on the second and fourth lines: proof/roof, I/cry, merriment/went, voice/rejoice. The final rhyme pairs the owl's 'voice' with 'rejoice', but the line denies rejoicing. The Cambridge Companion chapter reads the owl's cry as undermining the closing rhyme. The plain, conversational syntax and the careful qualifications are typical of Thomas's style, which Frost helped shape.
